title: EXCEPT & Set Difference
description: Find rows present in one query but absent in another using the EXCEPT set difference operator.

data.text: **`EXCEPT`** (equivalent to `MINUS` in Oracle) returns all distinct rows that appear in the first query result set but **do not** appear in the second query result set.

data.title: Finding Active Subscribers Who Have Not Opened Any Newsletters
data.content: Excluding engaged users using set difference.

data.text: EXCEPT ALL and the NOT EXISTS Rewrite

`EXCEPT` removes duplicates, so it can hide information about how many times a row appeared. `EXCEPT ALL` (PostgreSQL 15 and later) subtracts multiplicities instead, which is useful when counts matter. For large tables, an anti-join with `NOT EXISTS` is often the faster and more index-friendly form.

data.title: Two ways to express a set difference
data.content: The first query keeps duplicates in the difference; the second uses an anti-join and can stop at the first matching row per id.
data.code:
-- Multiplicity-aware difference (PostgreSQL 15+)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM all_events

EXCEPT ALL

SELECT user_id
FROM engaged_users;

-- Index-friendly anti-join equivalent
SELECT DISTINCT e.user_id
FROM all_events AS e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM engaged_users AS u
    WHERE u.user_id = e.user_id
);

data.title: Interview angle: EXCEPT and NULL
data.text: Set operators treat NULLs as equal to each other, unlike comparison or join predicates where NULL is never equal to NULL. So `EXCEPT` considers a NULL equal to another NULL for the purpose of duplicate elimination, while a `NOT IN` with NULLs silently returns no rows. Mentioning that difference is a strong signal that you understand three-valued logic.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `EXCEPT` subtracts the second query's rows from the first query's result set.
Removes duplicates by default; `EXCEPT ALL` retains duplicates.
Useful for quick ad-hoc difference checks across identical schemas.
